courses.title: AI Fundamentals & Prompting
courses.subtitle: What modern AI really is — and how to get great results from it
courses.description: Artificial intelligence is changing how people learn and work. This course explains, in plain language, what AI systems actually do, where they fail, and how to write prompts that produce useful, reliable results.

courses.title: Blender: Your First Steps in 3D
courses.subtitle: From “what is 3D?” to confidently moving around your first scene
courses.description:
Blender is a free, open-source application used for 3D modeling, animation, visual effects and rendering — by hobbyists and professional studios alike.

This course begins before Blender: you will first understand **what 3D actually is**. Then you will install Blender, learn its interface and move, rotate and scale objects with the same shortcuts professionals use.
learning_outcomes: Explain vertices, edges, faces and the X/Y/Z axes
Install Blender and identify the main areas of the interface
Navigate the 3D viewport with mouse, keyboard and gizmo
Add, move, rotate and scale objects precisely
prerequisites: A computer with a dedicated or recent integrated graphics chip

courses.title: Computer Fundamentals from Zero
courses.subtitle: Understand the machine in front of you — no prior knowledge needed
courses.description:
This course assumes **nothing**. If you have ever wondered what actually happens inside a computer, why files have strange endings like `.pdf`, or what people mean by “hardware” and “software”, you are in the right place.

You will build a clear mental model of how a computer takes in information, works on it, stores it and shows you the result. Every term is explained the first time it appears.
learning_outcomes: Explain what a computer is using the input → processing → storage → output model
Tell hardware and software apart and name the main parts of a computer
Understand bits and bytes and read storage sizes like GB and TB
Navigate files, folders and paths with confidence
prerequisites: No prior knowledge — just curiosity and access to any computer

courses.title: Design Principles from Zero
courses.subtitle: Why some designs feel effortless — and how to make yours feel that way
courses.description: Good design is not decoration; it is communication. This course teaches the principles behind clear, beautiful work — hierarchy, contrast, alignment, proximity, repetition and white space — so you can judge and improve any poster, slide, website or app.
learning_outcomes: Create a clear visual hierarchy
Use contrast, alignment and proximity deliberately
Critique a layout using precise vocabulary

courses.title: HTML from Absolute Zero
courses.subtitle: Build your first real web page — and understand every line of it
courses.description:
HTML is the language every web page is written in. In this course you start with **how the web works**, then write a complete page by hand.

No installs are needed beyond a text editor and a browser you already have. Each lesson explains the *why* before the *how*, so you understand the code instead of copying it.
learning_outcomes: Explain what happens between typing an address and seeing a page
Write a valid HTML document from memory
Structure content with headings, paragraphs and lists
Publish-ready habits: indentation, semantic tags and comments
prerequisites: Basic computer use: creating a file and opening it

courses.title: Python for Complete Beginners
courses.subtitle: Your first programming language, explained without jargon
courses.description:
Python is one of the most popular programming languages in the world — used for automation, data science, AI, websites and teaching. It reads almost like English, which makes it an excellent first language.

This course starts with **what programming is** before you write a single line, then moves step by step through installing Python, running programs and working with values.
learning_outcomes: Explain what a program is and how a computer runs it
Install Python and run code in the terminal and in files
Store and change information with variables
Recognise the basic data types: text, whole numbers, decimals and true/false
prerequisites: Computer Fundamentals from Zero, or equivalent confidence with files and folders

contents.body_md:
## A machine that follows instructions

A **computer** is a machine that takes in information, follows a list of instructions to work with that information, and gives you a result. That’s it. Your laptop, your phone, a smartwatch, a cash register and the servers that run websites are all computers.

What makes computers special is not that they are clever — they are not. They are **extremely fast** and **perfectly obedient**. A modern computer can follow billions of simple instructions every second, exactly as written.

> [!NOTE]
> The list of instructions a computer follows is called a **program**. Writing programs is called **programming**.

## The four jobs of every computer

Every computer, no matter its size, does the same four jobs:

1. **Input** — receiving information. Typing on a keyboard, tapping a screen, speaking into a microphone or taking a photo are all input.
2. **Processing** — working on that information by following instructions. Adding numbers, applying a photo filter or checking a password are processing.
3. **Storage** — keeping information so it can be used later. Your photos, documents and installed apps are stored.
4. **Output** — showing or sending the result. Text on a screen, sound from a speaker, a printed page or a message sent to a friend are output.

## An everyday example

When you take a photo with your phone:

- the camera captures light — **input**
- the phone improves colours and sharpness — **processing**
- the photo is saved to the gallery — **storage**
- the photo appears on your screen — **output**

> [!TIP]
> Whenever a new technology feels confusing, ask: *what is the input, what processing happens, what is stored, and what is the output?* This one question explains a surprising amount of computing.

## Key terms

- **Computer** — a machine that follows instructions to process information.
- **Program** — a list of instructions for a computer.
- **Input / Output** — information going into / coming out of a computer.

## Two halves of every computer

Every computer is made of two kinds of things:

- **Hardware** — the physical parts you could touch: the screen, keyboard, chips and cables.
- **Software** — the instructions (programs) that tell the hardware what to do: the operating system, a web browser, a game.

Hardware without software is a box that does nothing. Software without hardware has nowhere to run. You need both.

## The main hardware parts

| Part | What it does | A simple comparison |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **CPU** (processor) | Follows instructions — the “thinking” part | A chef following a recipe |
| **RAM** (memory) | Holds what you are working on *right now* | The chef’s worktable |
| **Storage** (SSD or hard drive) | Keeps files and apps even when power is off | The pantry |
| **GPU** (graphics processor) | Draws images, video and 3D quickly | A specialist pastry chef |
| **Motherboard** | Connects every part so they can communicate | The kitchen itself |
| **Power supply / battery** | Provides electricity | The gas line |

> [!NOTE]
> **RAM is temporary.** When the power goes off, whatever is only in RAM disappears. That is why you *save* your work — saving copies it from RAM to storage.

## Kinds of software

- **Operating system (OS)** — the main program that manages the hardware and runs everything else. Examples: Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS.
- **Applications (apps)** — programs that help you do a task: a browser, a photo editor, a messenger.
- **Drivers** — small programs that let the operating system talk to a specific piece of hardware, such as a printer.

## Bits and bytes

Inside the computer, all information — text, photos, music — is stored as numbers made of only two digits, **0** and **1**. One such digit is a **bit**.

- 8 bits = 1 **byte** (enough to store one simple letter like “A”)
- about 1,000 bytes = 1 **kilobyte (KB)**
- about 1,000 KB = 1 **megabyte (MB)** — a typical photo is a few MB
- about 1,000 MB = 1 **gigabyte (GB)** — a film is a few GB
- about 1,000 GB = 1 **terabyte (TB)**

> [!TIP]
> When buying a computer, *storage* (e.g. 512 GB SSD) tells you how much you can keep, while *RAM* (e.g. 16 GB) tells you how much you can work on at the same time.

## What is a file?

A **file** is a single piece of stored information with a name: a document, a photo, a song, a program. Files live on storage (your SSD or hard drive, a USB stick, or the cloud).

Most file names end with a dot and a few letters, for example `report.pdf` or `holiday.jpg`. That ending is the **file extension**. It tells the computer what kind of file it is and which app should open it.

| Extension | Kind of file |
| --- | --- |
| `.pdf` | Document that looks the same everywhere |
| `.docx` | Word document |
| `.jpg`, `.png` | Image |
| `.mp4` | Video |
| `.mp3` | Audio |
| `.zip` | Several files compressed into one |

> [!WARNING]
> Renaming `photo.jpg` to `photo.mp4` does **not** turn a photo into a video. It only confuses the computer about which app to use.

## Folders

A **folder** (also called a *directory*) is a container for files and other folders. Folders inside folders create a tree:

```text
Documents
├── School
│   ├── math-homework.pdf
│   └── essay.docx
└── Work
    └── invoice-march.pdf
```

## Paths: a file’s address

A **path** is the full address of a file — every folder you pass through to reach it.

- On **Windows**: `C:\Users\Aziza\Documents\School\essay.docx`
- On **macOS** and **Linux**: `/Users/aziza/Documents/School/essay.docx`

Read it left to right like an address: drive or root → user → folder → sub-folder → file. Windows uses a backslash `\` between folders; macOS and Linux use a forward slash `/`.

> [!TIP]
> Good habits that professionals use:
> - Use clear names: `invoice-2026-03.pdf` beats `scan1 final FINAL.pdf`.
> - Put dates as `YYYY-MM-DD` so files sort in order.
> - Avoid spaces and special symbols in names for files you will use in code or on the web.
> - Keep a backup of important files in a second place.

## Five steps from address to page

When you type `example.com` and press Enter, this happens in well under a second:

1. **Your browser asks for the address.** Computers on the internet find each other by numbers called *IP addresses*. A system called **DNS** works like a phone book and turns `example.com` into a number.
2. **The browser sends a request.** It contacts the computer at that address — a **server** — and asks: “Please send me your home page.” This conversation follows rules called **HTTP** (or **HTTPS** when it is encrypted — look for the padlock).
3. **The server responds** with files: an **HTML** file, usually some **CSS** and **JavaScript**, plus images and fonts.
4. **The browser reads the HTML** from top to bottom and builds the structure of the page.
5. **The browser paints the page** on your screen, applying styles and running scripts.

## The three languages of the web

| Language | Job | Comparison with a house |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **HTML** | Structure and content | Walls, rooms and furniture |
| **CSS** | Appearance and layout | Paint, lighting and decoration |
| **JavaScript** | Behaviour and interaction | Electricity, doors that open, the doorbell |

> [!NOTE]
> HTML is not a programming language in the strict sense — it does not make decisions or repeat steps. It is a **markup language**: it *labels* content so the browser knows what each piece is.

## Key terms

- **Browser** — the app that requests and displays web pages (Chrome, Safari, Firefox, Edge).
- **Server** — a computer that stores a website and sends it on request.
- **URL** — the full address of a page, such as `https://example.com/about`.

## Labelling content HTML stands for **HyperText Markup Language**. You write normal text and wrap each part in **tags** that say what it is. ```html

My first page

Hello! This is a paragraph.

``` - `

` means “a top-level heading starts here”. - `

` — with a slash — means “the heading ends here”. - The opening tag, the content and the closing tag together form an **element**. ## Attributes add extra information Some elements need more details. These go inside the opening tag as **attributes**, written `name="value"`: ```html Visit Example ``` - `href` tells a link where to go. - `src` tells an image which file to show. - `alt` describes the image for people using screen readers, and appears if the image fails to load. > [!TIP] > Always write a meaningful `alt`. It is required for accessibility and helps search engines understand your page. ## Elements can contain other elements ```html

This is very important.

``` Here `` lives *inside* `

`. Close tags in the reverse order you opened them — like nesting boxes. > [!WARNING] > Overlapping tags like `

text

` are a mistake. Browsers try to guess what you meant, but the result is unpredictable. ## Empty elements A few elements have no content and no closing tag, for example `` and `
` (a line break).

## The skeleton of every page Every HTML document has the same basic structure. Read each line and its explanation: ```html My first page

Hello, web!

I wrote this page myself.

``` - `` — tells the browser this is modern HTML. - `` — the root element; `lang` declares the page language (use `uz` for Uzbek, `ru` for Russian). - `` — information *about* the page that is not shown directly. - `` — lets the page display every alphabet and emoji correctly. - `` — makes the page fit phone screens. - `` — the text on the browser tab. - `<body>` — everything visible on the page. ## Try it yourself 1. Open a plain text editor — *Notepad* on Windows, *TextEdit* on macOS (choose **Format → Make Plain Text**), or a code editor such as VS Code. 2. Type the code above. Typing it, rather than pasting it, helps you remember it. 3. Save the file as `index.html`. Make sure the extension is `.html`, not `.txt`. 4. Double-click the file. It opens in your browser. 5. Change the heading text, save, and refresh the browser to see your change. > [!TIP] > Indent elements that are inside other elements by two spaces. Browsers ignore the spaces, but people reading your code — including future you — will thank you. When you can explain what each line does, take the knowledge check below.

## Headings create an outline HTML has six heading levels, `

` to `

`. They are not about size — they describe **importance and structure**, like chapters and sections in a book. ```html

Learning to cook

Breakfast

Omelette

Porridge

Dinner

``` > [!TIP] > Use exactly one `

` per page and never skip levels (do not jump from `

` to `

`). Screen-reader users navigate by headings, and search engines read them to understand your page. ## Paragraphs Wrap each block of text in `

`. Browsers ignore extra spaces and line breaks in your code, so pressing Enter in the editor does **not** create a new paragraph — a new `

` does. ## Lists **Unordered lists** (bullets) are for items where order does not matter: ```html

  • Flour
  • Eggs
  • Milk
``` **Ordered lists** (numbers) are for steps where order matters: ```html
  1. Crack the eggs
  2. Whisk with milk
  3. Cook for three minutes
``` `
  • ` means *list item*, and it must always be inside a `
      ` or `
        `. ## Emphasis with meaning - `` — strong importance (shown in bold by default). - `` — stress emphasis, as when you change your tone of voice (shown in italics). These carry *meaning*. If you only want a visual style, that is a job for CSS.

## Your first project

Build a single page called `index.html` that introduces you (or a fictional person). It must use what you have learned — and nothing more is expected.

### Requirements

1. A valid document skeleton with `lang`, `charset`, `viewport` and a `<title>`.
2. Exactly one `<h1>` with the person’s name.
3. At least two `<h2>` sections, for example *About me* and *Skills I am learning*.
4. At least two paragraphs.
5. One unordered list and one ordered list (e.g. *My goals for this year*, in order).
6. At least one `<strong>` and one `<em>` used for meaning.
7. Neat indentation.

### How to submit

Paste your HTML code in the text box, **or** upload your `index.html` file, **or** share a link if you have published it (for example with GitHub Pages).

> [!NOTE]
> A reviewer checks your work against the rubric and leaves feedback. You can resubmit after making changes.

## Precise recipes

A **program** is a list of instructions. **Programming** is the skill of writing those instructions so precisely that a machine with zero common sense can follow them.

Imagine explaining to a robot how to make tea. “Make tea” is not enough. You would need: *fill the kettle with water, switch it on, wait until it boils, put a tea bag in a cup, pour the water…* — every step, in order, with nothing left out. That is how programmers think.

## Why programming languages exist

Computers only understand very simple numeric instructions. Writing those directly is slow and error-prone. **Programming languages** like Python let you write instructions in readable words, and a special program translates them for the computer.

```python
print("Hello, world!")
```

This single line tells the computer to display the text `Hello, world!`. Almost every programmer’s first program does exactly this.

## Three ideas you will use forever

1. **Sequence** — instructions run one after another, top to bottom.
2. **Decisions** — do something only *if* a condition is true.
3. **Repetition** — do something many times without writing it many times.

> [!TIP]
> Mistakes in code are called **bugs**, and fixing them is **debugging**. Every programmer — including experts — writes bugs every day. Error messages are not failures; they are clues.

## 1. Install Python

- **Windows:** download the latest *Python 3* installer from **python.org**. On the first screen of the installer, tick **“Add python.exe to PATH”**, then click *Install Now*.
- **macOS:** download the macOS installer from **python.org** and run it.
- **Linux:** Python 3 is usually already installed.

> [!WARNING]
> Only download Python from the official site, **python.org**. Unofficial download sites sometimes bundle unwanted software.

## 2. Open a terminal

A **terminal** is a window where you type commands instead of clicking.

- Windows: open the Start menu and search for **Terminal** (or *Command Prompt*).
- macOS: open **Terminal** from Applications → Utilities.

Check the installation:

```bash
python --version
```

On macOS and Linux you may need `python3 --version`. You should see something like `Python 3.13.1`.

## 3. Run code interactively

Type `python` (or `python3`) and press Enter. The prompt changes to `>>>`. Now type:

```python
>>> 2 + 3
5
>>> print("Salom, dunyo!")
Salom, dunyo!
```

Type `exit()` to leave.

## 4. Run a program from a file

Create a file called `hello.py` with this content:

```python
name = "Aziz"
print("Hello,", name)
print("Welcome to Python.")
```

In the terminal, go to the folder with the file and run:

```bash
python hello.py
```

> [!TIP]
> Interactive mode is perfect for quick experiments. Files are for programs you want to keep and run again.

## Order of importance

**Visual hierarchy** is the arrangement of elements so that people notice them in order of importance. In a well-designed poster you see the title first, then the key detail (date, price), and only then the small print — without trying.

## Tools that create hierarchy

- **Size** — bigger elements are seen first.
- **Weight** — bold text stands out from regular text.
- **Colour and contrast** — a bright accent on a calm background draws attention.
- **Position** — people in left-to-right languages tend to start at the top left.
- **Space** — an element surrounded by empty space feels important.

> [!TIP]
> **The squint test:** squint at your design until it blurs. Whatever still stands out is what people will notice first. If that is not the most important thing, adjust the hierarchy.

## One focal point

If everything is bold, nothing is. Choose **one** primary element per screen or page, support it with one or two secondary elements, and keep everything else quiet.

## A labelled box

A **variable** is a name that refers to a value — like a labelled box you can put something into.

```python
age = 17
city = "Samarkand"
```

The `=` sign does **not** mean “equals” as in maths. It means *“store the value on the right under the name on the left”*. Read it as “age **becomes** 17”.

You can change a variable later:

```python
age = 17
age = age + 1
print(age)  # 18
```

The text after `#` is a **comment** — a note for humans that Python ignores.

## The basic types

| Type | Name in Python | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Text | `str` (string) | `"Hello"` |
| Whole number | `int` (integer) | `42` |
| Decimal number | `float` | `3.14` |
| True / false | `bool` (boolean) | `True` |

Ask Python for a value’s type with `type()`:

```python
print(type("Hello"))  # <class 'str'>
print(type(42))       # <class 'int'>
```

## Naming rules

- Use letters, digits and underscores: `total_price`, `player2`.
- Do not start with a digit: `2player` is invalid.
- Names are case-sensitive: `Age` and `age` are different variables.
- Choose names that explain themselves: `minutes_per_day` beats `m`.

## Practice

Predict what this program prints **before** you run it:

```python
apples = 5
apples = apples * 2
price = 1.5
print(apples * price)
```

Then run it. Did you predict `15.0`? Multiplying an `int` by a `float` produces a `float`.

## Three nested ideas

- **Artificial intelligence (AI)** is the broad goal: computers performing tasks that normally require human intelligence, such as understanding language or recognising images.
- **Machine learning (ML)** is one way to achieve it: instead of writing every rule by hand, we show a computer many examples and it *learns patterns* from them.
- **Deep learning** is a kind of machine learning that uses large **neural networks** — layered mathematical models loosely inspired by the brain.

## Learning from examples

A spam filter is a classic example. Nobody writes a rule for every possible spam message. Instead, the system sees millions of emails labelled “spam” or “not spam” and learns which patterns usually mean spam.

## What AI is not

> [!WARNING]
> Today’s AI systems do not *understand* the world the way people do, and they have no intentions. They produce outputs based on patterns in their training data. That makes them powerful — and capable of confident mistakes.

## Where you already meet AI

Photo search on your phone, voice assistants, translation apps, recommendations on video platforms, and chat assistants that can write and explain text.

## Predicting the next piece of text

A **large language model (LLM)** is trained on a huge amount of text. Its core skill is surprisingly simple to state: given some text, **predict what comes next**.

Text is split into small pieces called **tokens** — whole words, parts of words or punctuation. The model repeatedly predicts the next token, adds it, and predicts again. Because it learned from so much writing, those predictions can form explanations, summaries, code and translations.

## Why this matters for you

- **Context is everything.** The model only knows what is in its training and what you put in the conversation. Give it the background it needs.
- **It can be wrong, fluently.** When a model produces believable but false information, this is called a **hallucination**.
- **It has a knowledge cut-off.** Unless connected to search or documents, it may not know recent events.

> [!TIP]
> Treat AI output like a draft from a fast, well-read assistant: useful, but **verify facts, numbers, quotes and sources** before you rely on them.

## From vague to precise

A vague prompt gets a generic answer:

> Write about Samarkand.

A structured prompt gets a useful one. Include these five parts:

1. **Role** — who should the assistant act as? *“You are a friendly history teacher.”*
2. **Context** — the background. *“My students are 14 and have never studied the Silk Road.”*
3. **Task** — exactly what you want. *“Explain why Samarkand became an important city.”*
4. **Constraints** — limits. *“Under 200 words, simple vocabulary, no dates except centuries.”*
5. **Format** — the shape of the answer. *“Three short paragraphs, then one question for discussion.”*

## Iterate

Your first prompt is a starting point. If the answer is too long, too formal or misses something, say so: *“Shorter, and add one example a teenager would relate to.”*

## Practice

Rewrite this weak prompt using all five parts, then try it with any AI assistant you have access to:

> Help me with my CV.

> [!NOTE]
> Never paste passwords, private documents or other people’s personal data into an AI tool unless you know exactly how that tool stores and uses it.

## Three directions

A drawing on paper is **2D**: it has width and height. The real world is **3D**: it also has depth. To describe any position in 3D space we need three numbers, one for each direction, called **axes**:

- **X** — left ↔ right
- **Y** — forward ↔ back
- **Z** — up ↔ down

> [!NOTE]
> In Blender, **Z points up**. Some other programs use Y as “up”, which matters when you move models between applications.

## What a 3D object is made of

Most 3D objects are **meshes** — surfaces built from three simple parts:

- **Vertex** (plural *vertices*) — a single point in space.
- **Edge** — a straight line between two vertices.
- **Face** — a flat surface enclosed by edges, usually with three or four sides.

A cube has 8 vertices, 12 edges and 6 faces. Even a detailed character is “just” many thousands of these.

## From model to image

Making a 3D image follows a pipeline that you will learn step by step in Mahorat courses:

1. **Modeling** — building the shape.
2. **Materials and texturing** — deciding what surfaces look like: metal, wood, skin.
3. **Lighting** — placing lights, just like on a film set.
4. **Camera** — choosing what the viewer sees.
5. **Rendering** — the computer calculates the final image from all of the above.

Add **animation** — changing things over time — and you can make films and games.

## A complete 3D studio

**Blender** is a free and open-source 3D creation suite developed by the Blender Foundation and a worldwide community. “Open source” means its code is public and anyone may use it — for personal or commercial work — without paying.

Blender covers the whole pipeline in one application:

- modeling and sculpting
- materials, texturing and UV unwrapping
- lighting and rendering with two engines: **EEVEE** (fast, real-time) and **Cycles** (physically accurate)
- animation and rigging
- simulations such as smoke, fluids and cloth
- video editing and compositing

## Who uses it?

Independent artists, game developers, product designers, architects and animation studios. Skills you learn in Blender — such as topology, lighting and composition — transfer to every other 3D application.

> [!TIP]
> Blender is updated often and menus move between versions. When instructions do not match your screen, check the version number on the splash screen and the official manual at docs.blender.org.

## Install

1. Go to **blender.org** and open the **Download** page.
2. Download the version for your system (Windows, macOS — choose Apple Silicon or Intel — or Linux).
3. Run the installer, then open Blender.

> [!WARNING]
> Download Blender only from blender.org (or official stores such as Steam and the Microsoft Store). It is free — any site asking for payment is not official.

## The default scene

Blender opens with a **cube**, a **camera** and a **light**. This is the default scene, ready for you to experiment.

## The five main areas

1. **3D Viewport** — the large central area where you see and edit your scene.
2. **Outliner** (top right) — a list of every object in the scene, like a table of contents.
3. **Properties Editor** (bottom right) — settings for the selected object, its material, the render and more, organised in tabs.
4. **Timeline** (bottom) — controls for animation over time.
5. **Toolbar** (left of the viewport) — tools such as Select, Move, Rotate and Scale.

Across the top are **workspaces** (Layout, Modeling, Sculpting, Shading…). Each is a pre-arranged set of areas for a particular job.

> [!TIP]
> Hover over almost any button and wait — Blender shows a tooltip explaining what it does.

## The three moves

| Action | Mouse | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Orbit** | Hold **middle mouse button** and drag | Rotates your view around the scene |
| **Pan** | **Shift** + middle mouse drag | Slides your view sideways |
| **Zoom** | Scroll the wheel | Moves closer or further away |

## Useful views (numeric keypad)

- **1** — front, **3** — right side, **7** — top
- **Ctrl** + the same key — the opposite side
- **0** — look through the camera
- **.** (period) on the keypad — frame the selected object

No keypad? Press the **` (backtick)** key for a pie menu of views, or click the axes in the **navigation gizmo** at the top right of the viewport.

> [!TIP]
> Using a laptop without a middle mouse button? Open **Edit → Preferences → Input** and enable **Emulate 3 Button Mouse**. Then **Alt + left-drag** orbits.

## Lost?

Press **Home** to fit everything in view.

## Adding objects

Press **Shift + A** in the viewport to open the **Add** menu. Choose **Mesh → UV Sphere**. New objects appear at the **3D cursor** (the red-and-white ring).

## Transforming

Select an object by left-clicking it, then:

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| **G** | Grab (move) |
| **R** | Rotate |
| **S** | Scale |

Move the mouse, then **left-click** to confirm or **right-click** (or Esc) to cancel.

## Constraining to an axis

After pressing G, R or S, press **X**, **Y** or **Z** to limit the change to that axis. You can also type a number:

- **G Z 2** → move 2 metres up
- **R X 90** → rotate 90° around the X axis
- **S 0.5** → scale to half size

## Undo and the sidebar

- **Ctrl + Z** undoes, **Ctrl + Shift + Z** redoes.
- Press **N** to open the **sidebar**, where you can type exact Location, Rotation and Scale values.

## Practice

Delete the default cube (**X → Delete**), then build a simple snowman: three UV spheres of decreasing size stacked along Z, plus a cone for the nose rotated 90° around X.

## Editing is storytelling

**Video editing** is selecting the best moments from recorded footage, putting them in an order and timing them so they tell a story or deliver a message. Editors decide what the audience sees, for how long, and in what sequence.

A finished two-minute video might come from an hour of footage. Most of editing is **choosing what to leave out**.

## Key vocabulary

- **Footage** — the raw recorded video.
- **Clip** — one piece of footage placed in your project.
- **Shot** — a continuous recording from one camera angle.
- **Cut** — the point where one shot ends and the next begins.
- **Sequence** — clips arranged together in order.

## Why cuts work

Our brains accept cuts naturally because we already “cut” our attention many times a minute when we look around. A good cut is often invisible: the viewer follows the story and never notices the edit.

> [!TIP]
> Watch a scene from a favourite film with the sound off and count the cuts. You will notice far more than you expected — and that most of them felt invisible.

## The timeline

Every editor has a **timeline**: time runs left to right, and clips sit on horizontal **tracks**.

- **Video tracks** are stacked: higher tracks appear *on top* of lower ones (useful for titles and overlays).
- **Audio tracks** sit below and play together.

The **playhead** is the vertical line that marks the current frame.

## Project settings

| Setting | Common values | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Resolution** | 1920×1080 (Full HD), 3840×2160 (4K) | Number of pixels in each frame |
| **Frame rate** | 24, 25, 30, 60 fps | Images shown per second |
| **Aspect ratio** | 16:9 (landscape), 9:16 (vertical), 1:1 | Shape of the frame |

> [!NOTE]
> Choose the frame rate before you start and keep it consistent. 24 fps feels cinematic, 25 is common for broadcast in many countries, and 60 is smooth for sports and games.

## Types of cut

- **Hard cut** — a straight switch from one shot to the next. The most common edit.
- **Jump cut** — a cut within the same shot that skips time; popular in vlogs.
- **J-cut** — the *audio* of the next shot starts before its video.
- **L-cut** — the audio of the current shot continues over the next shot’s video.
- **Cutaway** — briefly showing something else (a detail, a reaction) before returning.

## A professional workflow

1. **Organise** — import and name your footage in folders (bins).
2. **Assembly** — place the usable shots roughly in order.
3. **Rough cut** — shape the story; get the structure right.
4. **Fine cut** — perfect the timing of every cut.
5. **Colour and sound** — correct, grade and mix.
6. **Export** — render the final file for its destination.

## Not starting from nothing

Every game needs to draw images, play sounds, read the controller, simulate physics and load levels. Writing all of that from scratch would take years. A **game engine** is a ready-made foundation that provides these systems so creators can focus on *their* game.

## What an engine typically provides

- **Rendering** — drawing 3D worlds in real time, many times per second.
- **Physics** — gravity, collisions and objects that fall and bounce.
- **Input** — keyboard, mouse, gamepad and touch.
- **Audio** — positional sound and music.
- **Scripting** — ways to describe game rules and behaviour.
- **Tools** — an editor to build levels and manage assets.

## Unreal Engine in particular

Unreal Engine is developed by Epic Games. Version 5 introduced systems such as **Nanite** (very detailed geometry) and **Lumen** (dynamic global illumination). Behaviour can be built with **Blueprints**, a visual node-based system, or written in **C++**.

> [!NOTE]
> Unreal Engine is free to download and learn. Commercial releases are subject to Epic’s licence terms — always read the current EULA on unrealengine.com before publishing a product.

## Contrast

**Contrast** is difference: large vs small, dark vs light, bold vs thin. Contrast creates interest and tells people which things are different. Make differences **obvious** — two font sizes that are almost the same look like a mistake.

> [!WARNING]
> Text must contrast strongly with its background to be readable. Accessibility guidelines (WCAG) recommend a contrast ratio of at least **4.5 : 1** for normal body text.

## Alignment

**Alignment** means placing elements along shared invisible lines. Aligned elements look connected and organised; randomly placed elements look careless. Pick one alignment (for example, everything left-aligned to the same edge) and stick to it.

## Proximity

**Proximity** means related items belong close together, and unrelated items are separated by space. A caption sits right under its photo; a new section starts after a larger gap.

## Repetition and white space

- **Repetition** — reuse the same colours, fonts and spacing so the design feels like one system.
- **White space** — empty space is not wasted space. It gives content room to breathe and makes everything easier to read.
